scaffold-overview.title: Introduction to Supported Scaffold Safety
scaffold-overview.content: Supported scaffolds are elevated work platforms held up by rigid supports such as poles, legs, uprights, posts, frames, or similar structural members. They provide larger work areas than ladders and can safely support workers, tools, and materials when properly constructed and used. Major scaffold hazards include falls from elevation, falling tools or materials, scaffold collapse, unsafe access, electrical contact, overloading, poor housekeeping, improper assembly or disassembly, and damaged or incompatible parts. OSHA requires scaffold users to receive appropriate training before working on scaffolds. A scaffold expert, competent person, or qualified individual must oversee scaffold design, erection, inspection, problem-solving, and safety enforcement.

roles-supervision.title: Scaffold Roles, Responsibilities, and Supervision
roles-supervision.content: Not every employee is qualified to erect, alter, move, dismantle, or inspect a scaffold. Workers who use scaffolds must know how to access the scaffold safely, recognize obvious hazards, avoid unsafe work practices, report defects, use fall protection when required, and avoid overloading platforms. A scaffold expert or competent person is responsible for supervising erection and dismantling, inspecting components, evaluating supporting surfaces, determining fall protection requirements, ensuring the scaffold meets design requirements, and correcting unsafe conditions. Employees must not modify scaffold components, remove guardrails, move planks, overload platforms, or use makeshift access methods unless authorized and trained. Unsafe scaffold use often occurs when employees assume they can make a quick adjustment without authorization.

safe-access.title: Safe Scaffold Access and Inspection
safe-access.content: Workers must use designated access points including ladders, stairway towers, ramps, walkways, and built-in scaffold access systems. Workers must never climb scaffold crossbraces — crossbraces are not designed to provide safe handholds or footholds and climbing them can destabilize the scaffold. Access ladders should be secured to the scaffold and extend above the platform when required. Workers using ladders must maintain three points of contact: two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand. Scaffold access points and platforms should be inspected before use and throughout the shift. Employees should look for damaged ladders, loose or missing rails, slippery surfaces, missing or damaged planks, debris or clutter, and unsafe material storage. Any defect must be reported immediately — workers should not use a scaffold that appears unsafe.

fall-protection-falling-objects.title: Fall Protection and Falling Object Prevention
fall-protection-falling-objects.content: Falls are one of the most serious scaffold hazards. Guardrail systems prevent workers from stepping or falling off open sides. Personal fall arrest systems — including anchorage, full-body harness, connector, lifeline, and deceleration device — stop a worker after a fall begins. Anchor points must be approved for fall arrest use; workers must not tie off to weak or unauthorized scaffold components. Guardrails must not be removed even temporarily. Falling object protection may include toe boards, screens, guardrail mesh, debris nets, tool lanyards, barricades, and controlled access zones below the scaffold. Toe boards create a barrier at the platform edge to prevent tools from sliding off. Workers should never throw materials from a scaffold. Hard hats must be worn where overhead hazards or falling objects may be present, but they are the last line of defense — engineering controls come first.

foundations-components.title: Scaffold Foundations, Bases, and Component Compatibility
foundations-components.content: A supported scaffold is only as stable as the surface it rests on. The supporting surface must carry the scaffold and its maximum intended load — including workers, tools, materials, equipment, scaffold components, and any forces applied to the scaffold — without settling, shifting, or collapsing. Scaffold legs may be fitted with adjustable screw jacks and mud sills or base plates to distribute weight and prevent sinking into soil. Improvised supports such as cinder blocks, bricks, scrap lumber, buckets, or stacked materials must never be used as scaffold foundations. Scaffold components from different manufacturers must not be mixed unless a qualified person determines they are compatible. Damaged, bent, cracked, corroded, or missing components must be removed from service. Parts that must be forced together indicate an incompatibility that can create structural hazards.

platforms-planking.title: Scaffold Platforms and Planking
platforms-planking.content: Scaffold platforms may be made of wood, metal, or approved manufactured materials designed for scaffold use. Planks must be inspected before use and at the beginning of each shift for cracks, splits, warping, rot, loose hooks or fittings, excessive wear, oil, mud, ice, slippery surfaces, burn marks, and damage. Painted planks should generally not be used because paint can hide damage and may become slippery. Gaps between planks should be minimized to reduce tripping and falling-object hazards. Planks must rest properly on scaffold supports — overextended planks can tip if workers step on the unsupported end, while underextended planks can shift or fall. Where planks overlap, they must overlap sufficiently to remain secure. Platforms must be wide enough for the work, worker movement, and materials while maintaining fall protection and safe access.

work-practices-overhead.title: Safe Work Practices and Overhead Hazards
work-practices-overhead.content: Workers should work from stable positions and never lean outside the scaffold, climb guardrails, stand on toe boards, use boxes or buckets, or stretch beyond safe reach. If the work is beyond safe reach, reposition the scaffold. Materials must be stored safely and not overload the platform. Work should stop if weather, vibration, equipment movement, or jobsite conditions make scaffold use unsafe. Power lines are one of the most dangerous hazards near scaffolds. Both workers and scaffold components must maintain required clearance distances from energized power lines — the higher the voltage, the greater the required clearance. Workers must also watch for overhead beams, pipes, ductwork, moving cranes, suspended loads, sprinkler lines, and low ceilings. Never assume a power line is de-energized unless the utility or responsible authority has confirmed it. Metal scaffold components, tools, and materials can all conduct electricity.

1.questionText: Which description best fits a supported scaffold?

options.text: A platform that hangs from an overhead structure by ropes
A vehicle-mounted platform that can be raised and lowered
A work platform built up from the ground and supported by rigid structural members
A type of aerial lift attached to a forklift

2.questionText: Climbing scaffold crossbraces is an acceptable way to reach a scaffold platform when no ladder is nearby.

options.text: True
False

3.questionText: Which access method is specifically designed and approved for climbing onto a scaffold platform?

options.text: Scaffold crossbrace
Exterior scaffold frame
Secured access ladder, ramp, or stairway tower
Nearby forklift forks

4.questionText: How many points of contact must a worker maintain while climbing a scaffold ladder?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

5.questionText: Which of the following scaffold defects must be reported before use?

options.text: A missing guardrail only
An unstable base only
A cracked plank only
All scaffold defects must be reported before use

6.questionText: Wearing a hard hat provides some protection from falling-object hazards on and around scaffolds.

options.text: True
False

7.questionText: What does a toe board on a scaffold platform help prevent?

options.text: Workers from stepping off the edge
Tools and materials from rolling or sliding off the platform edge
The scaffold from shifting on its base
Workers from overloading the platform

8.questionText: A cracked scaffold plank is found before a shift begins. What is the correct action?

options.text: Use it for light-duty tasks only
Secure the crack with tape and inspect again after the shift
Remove it from service and notify the supervisor or competent person
Place it in the center of the platform away from the edges

9.questionText: What makes a painted scaffold plank hazardous for scaffold use?

options.text: The added weight of paint can overload scaffold supports
Paint conceals cracks and defects, and the surface may be slippery
OSHA requires all scaffold planks to be left unpainted by regulation
Paint causes the wood to absorb moisture and warp more quickly

10.questionText: Which scaffold foundation method creates a collapse hazard?

options.text: Using base plates with mud sills on soft ground
Leveling the scaffold with properly adjusted screw jacks
Supporting scaffold legs on stacked cinder blocks or scrap lumber
Clearing and leveling the ground before erection

11.questionText: A worker is standing on a scaffold guardrail to reach work that is slightly beyond the platform edge. What corrective action is appropriate?

options.text: Allow it as long as the worker keeps one hand on a fixed support
Provide a spotter to hold the worker steady
Reposition the scaffold or use another approved means of reaching the work area safely
Place a bucket on the platform for the worker to stand on instead

12.questionText: A wrench slides off a scaffold platform and falls to the ground without injuring anyone. What is the proper response?

options.text: No action is needed since no injury occurred
Report it as a near miss and assess controls such as toe boards or tool lanyards
Mention it briefly during the end-of-day crew discussion
Monitor for a pattern before reporting to supervision

13.questionText: What is one of the most dangerous overhead hazards when erecting or working on scaffolds outdoors?

options.text: Overhead power lines
Direct sunlight or glare
Birds nesting on overhead structures
Low-hanging tree branches

14.questionText: It is acceptable to remove a scaffold guardrail temporarily if it interferes with work, as long as it is replaced after the task is complete.

options.text: True
False

15.questionText: If scaffold parts from two different manufacturers are available on-site, who determines whether they can be used together?

options.text: Any experienced scaffold worker
The site foreman based on past use of similar parts
A qualified person or competent scaffold expert
The purchasing department that ordered the parts
